stem: Which register transfer is the first step of the fetch stage?

options.content: MAR ← [PC]
options.rationale: Correct: the address of the next instruction is copied from the PC to the MAR.

options.content: PC ← [MDR]
options.rationale: The PC does not take its value from the MDR in a normal fetch.

options.content: CIR ← [MAR]
options.rationale: The CIR receives the instruction from the MDR, after it has been read.

options.content: MDR ← [PC]
options.rationale: The MDR holds data read from memory, not the address in the PC.

explanation: Fetch begins by copying the PC into the MAR.

stem: What happens to the program counter during the fetch stage?

options.content: It is increased by one to point to the next instruction
options.rationale: Correct: this happens before the instruction is executed.

options.content: It is set to zero so the program starts again
options.rationale: It is reset only by a jump or by starting a program.

options.content: It is copied to the accumulator
options.rationale: The accumulator holds data, not the PC.

options.content: It is not changed until the instruction has been executed
options.rationale: The PC is increased in the fetch stage.

explanation: PC ← [PC] + 1 is the second step of the fetch.

stem: What is the purpose of an interrupt?

options.content: To make the processor run faster for a short period
options.rationale: An interrupt does not increase the speed of the processor.

options.content: To copy data from the hard disk into the cache
options.rationale: That is a data transfer, not the purpose of an interrupt.

options.content: To make the processor pause and deal with an event
options.rationale: Correct: urgent events are handled by a special routine.

options.content: To remove errors from a program before it is run
options.rationale: Errors are found by testing and translators, not by interrupts.

explanation: An interrupt signals that something needs attention, so the processor runs an interrupt service routine.

stem: At which point does the processor check for interrupts?

options.content: At the start of the program only, never later
options.rationale: Interrupts can occur at any time and are checked all the time.

options.content: Halfway through each of the instructions
options.rationale: The current instruction is always completed first.

options.content: Only at the moment when the program ends
options.rationale: The program may need to be interrupted before it ends.

options.content: After each instruction is done
options.rationale: Correct: it never stops in the middle of an instruction.

explanation: The control unit checks for pending interrupts after each instruction is complete.

stem: Why are the contents of the PC and the other registers saved before an interrupt service routine runs?

options.content: So the ISR can run without using any registers at all
options.rationale: The ISR does use registers; that is why the old values are saved.

options.content: So the old program can carry on correctly
options.rationale: Correct: the registers are restored when the ISR finishes.

options.content: So the interrupt can be ignored later
options.rationale: The interrupt is handled, not ignored.

options.content: So the main program can be copied to the hard disk
options.rationale: Saving registers does not copy the program.

explanation: The ISR will overwrite registers and the PC, so their values are saved and later restored.
hints: What would be lost if the PC were overwritten by the ISR address?

stem: A program divides a number by zero and the processor signals an error. How does ZIMSEC classify this interrupt?

options.content: External
options.rationale: External interrupts come from hardware outside the processor.

options.content: Software, requested on purpose by a system call
options.rationale: A software interrupt is a deliberate request by a program.

options.content: Timer
options.rationale: Nothing here involves the timer.

options.content: Internal
options.rationale: Correct: it is caused by the running program inside the processor.

explanation: Division by zero and overflow are internal interrupts.
hints: Where does the cause of the interrupt come from?

stem: In register transfer notation, what does MDR ← [[MAR]] mean?

options.content: The address held in the MAR is copied to the MDR register
options.rationale: That would be written MDR ← [MAR] when [MAR] means the register contents.

options.content: The value in the MDR is copied into the MAR register
options.rationale: The arrow points to the MDR, so it is the destination.

options.content: The contents of the addressed location go to the MDR
options.rationale: Correct: the double brackets mean the contents of the addressed location.

options.content: The program counter is copied into the MDR register
options.rationale: The PC is not mentioned.

explanation: [MAR] is the address; [[MAR]] is the contents of memory at that address.
hints: One pair of brackets takes the contents of a register; two pairs take the contents of the location it points to.

stem: An interrupt service routine for a keyboard is running when a power failure interrupt of higher priority arrives. What should happen?

options.content: The power failure interrupt is ignored until the keyboard ISR ends
options.rationale: That would treat a lower-priority task as more important.

options.content: The processor stops and waits for the user to restart it
options.rationale: The processor deals with the interrupts itself.

options.content: The keyboard ISR is suspended and the power failure is done first
options.rationale: Correct: higher-priority interrupts are dealt with first.

options.content: Both ISRs run together on the same registers
options.rationale: One processor core runs one routine at a time.

explanation: Priorities decide the order. The state of the keyboard ISR is saved and restored once the more urgent interrupt is complete.
hints: Which of the two events is more urgent?

stem: When an interrupt occurs, the processor stops in the middle of the current instruction.
explanation: False. The current instruction is completed. The interrupt is detected at the end of the fetch-execute cycle.

stem: After an interrupt service routine has finished, the saved register values are restored.
explanation: True. Restoring the PC and the other registers lets the interrupted program continue exactly where it left off.

stem: Match each register transfer to its meaning.

right.content: The contents of the addressed location are read into the MDR
The instruction is placed in the current instruction register
The address of the next instruction is copied to the MAR
The PC is moved on to the next instruction

explanation: These four transfers are the fetch stage of the cycle.

stem: Complete the steps of handling an interrupt.

payload.template: The current instruction is {{blank:a}}. The contents of the registers are {{blank:b}}. The PC is loaded with the address of the {{blank:c}}. When it finishes, the registers are restored.

explanation: Complete, save, run the ISR, restore.

stem:
A program is stored from address 600:

```
600  LDM #6
601  ADD Rate
602  STO Pay
603  END
604  Rate: 4
605  Pay: 0
```

`LDM #6` loads the number 6 into the accumulator, `ADD Rate` adds the value stored at `Rate` to the accumulator and `STO Pay` stores the accumulator at `Pay`. What value is stored at `Pay` when the program ends?
explanation: 6 + 4 = 10 is stored at Pay.
workedSolution:
1. LDM #6: ACC = 6.
2. ADD Rate: ACC = 6 + 4 = 10.
3. STO Pay: address 605 holds 10.
hints: Follow the three instructions and keep the value in the accumulator.

stem: Name the routine that is run to deal with a particular interrupt.
explanation: The interrupt service routine (ISR) or interrupt handler deals with the interrupt.

stem: Write the four register transfers that make up the fetch stage of the fetch-execute cycle. [4]

answerSpec.markingNotes:
Example answer: MAR ← [PC]
PC ← [PC] + 1
MDR ← [[MAR]]
CIR ← [MDR]

explanation: One mark for each transfer in the correct order.
hints: Four lines: MAR, PC, MDR, CIR.

stem: Describe how the processor handles an interrupt that occurs while a program is running. [4]

points.description: The current instruction is completed and the interrupt is detected at the end of the cycle
The contents of the PC and the registers are saved (for example on a stack)
The PC is loaded with the address of the interrupt service routine, which then runs
The saved values are restored and the interrupted program continues

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The current instruction is finished and the interrupt is detected at the end of the cycle. The PC and registers are saved on a stack, then the PC is loaded with the address of the ISR. When the ISR has finished, the saved values are restored and the program carries on.

explanation: Detect, save, run the ISR, restore.

stem: Explain why the contents of the registers are saved before the interrupt service routine runs. [2]

points.description: The ISR will use the same registers and overwrite their contents
The saved values are restored afterwards so the interrupted program can continue correctly

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The ISR uses the registers and would overwrite their contents. Restoring the saved values lets the interrupted program continue as if nothing had happened.

explanation: Overwriting, then continuing correctly.

stem: Give three different causes of an interrupt. [3]

points.description: A hardware fault, such as a power failure
An input or output event, such as a key being pressed or a printer ready for data
A software error or request, such as division by zero, or a timer signal

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A power failure, a key being pressed, and a division by zero.

explanation: Any three different valid causes.

stem:
The program below is stored from address 500. The instruction at address 501 has just been fetched.

```
500  LDM #8
501  SUB Used
502  STO Left
503  END
504  Used: 3
505  Left: 0
```

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the contents of the PC, the MAR and the CIR after the fetch.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the value in the accumulator after the instruction at address 501 has been executed.
parts.workedSolution:
1. ACC was 8 after LDM #8.
2. SUB Used subtracts 3: 8 − 3 = 5.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State the value in the MAR when `STO Left` writes to memory.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Left is at address 505.
2. The MAR holds the address being written: 505.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Name the register that holds the instruction while it is being decoded.
parts.explanation: The CIR holds the instruction being decoded.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: An interrupt arrives while `SUB Used` is being executed. Explain why it is not handled until `SUB Used` is complete.

points.description: The processor completes the current instruction
Interrupts are checked at the end of each fetch-execute cycle

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The current instruction is always completed, and the check for interrupts takes place at the end of each fetch-execute cycle.

parts.explanation: Complete the instruction; check at the end.

explanation: After the fetch of the instruction at 501: PC 502, MAR 501, CIR SUB Used. ACC becomes 5, the MAR holds 505 when STO writes.
hints: The PC is increased during the fetch.
SUB uses direct addressing, so the MAR holds the address of Used.

stem: A school computer is running a spreadsheet when the user presses a key. The key press generates an interrupt.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: When does the processor check whether an interrupt has been signalled?

options.content: In the middle of every instruction
options.rationale: Instructions are completed first.

options.content: At the end of each fetch-execute cycle
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Only when the user switches off the computer
options.rationale: Interrupts are checked all the time the processor is running.

options.content: Only after the program has ended
options.rationale: The program must be able to be interrupted while it runs.

parts.explanation: The check takes place after each instruction is complete.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the program that is run to deal with the key press.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State what must be saved before the routine runs, and where it may be saved.

points.description: The contents of the PC and the registers in use
On a stack (or in a reserved area of memory)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The program counter and the registers, saved on a stack.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: While the keyboard routine is running, a power failure interrupt of higher priority occurs. Describe what the processor does.

points.description: It suspends the keyboard routine and saves its state
It handles the power failure first, then returns to the keyboard routine

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The keyboard routine is suspended and its state saved. The power failure routine runs first, and afterwards the keyboard routine resumes.

explanation: Interrupts are checked at the end of the cycle; the PC and registers are saved and restored; priority decides which interrupt is handled first.
hints: Think about what has to be restored afterwards.
